summary: McLatchie wins narrowly by offering the more developed comparative explanation, while Paulogia exposes serious unresolved dependence on Gospel proximity, transmission, and source-specific reliability.

pro.text: the best or most probable explanation is that Jesus rose from the dead
pro.context: McLatchie states his actual comparative conclusion in the final summary after distinguishing probability from logical necessity.

con.text: I think a naturalistic explanation is the best option
con.context: Paulogia closes by moving beyond mere possibility and explicitly endorsing a naturalistic explanation as comparatively preferable.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie reframed his obligation as comparative explanation: resurrection need only outperform live alternatives, not become deductively unavoidable, and this corrected Paulogia’s repeated use of required. Principal limitation: The clarification came after the opening burden had already drifted, however, and McLatchie still needed to specify a common measure by which textual reliability, sincere error, fabrication, and resurrection could be compared. Live burden: His remaining task was therefore to show that the maximal Gospel data deserved enough confidence and discriminative force to make the natural competitors less probable, while avoiding any inference from mere survival or unexplained detail. Locked score: 92/100 — Because he identified the proper motion-level standard clearly and used it consistently thereafter, yet left probability assignments implicit, this decisive correction earns 92 rather than a perfect score.
moves.words: McLatchie reframes the motion around comparative probability, correcting Paulogia’s repeated suggestion that resurrection must be logically required or uniquely possible in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia observed that Christian commitment cannot distinguish an accurate resurrection belief from a sincere but mistaken one, since either belief can motivate sacrifice, evangelism, and persistence across centuries. Principal limitation: That point sharply limits appeals to Christianity’s subsequent cultural success, but it says much less about the earliest named proclaimers whose access, experiences, and risks were the contested evidence. Live burden: He still had to connect motivational equivalence to a grounded origin scenario and demonstrate that an initial sincere error could generate the encounter traditions without relying only on abstract possibility. Locked score: 84/100 — The argument efficiently blocked an overinference from endurance to truth, while its reach stopped short of the earliest evidential links, so the locked score of 84 reflects strong relevance with incomplete explanatory development.
moves.words: Paulogia argues that accurate and mistaken resurrection beliefs can motivate identical commitment, limiting what later Christian endurance establishes about the initiating event.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: In his final synthesis, McLatchie presented a lucid trilemma—resurrection, honest mistake, or deceit—and connected mistake to multisensory encounters and deceit to costly proclamation, giving the cumulative case an intelligible structure. Principal limitation: Its force depended on treating the Gospel encounters as substantially unembellished testimony, precisely the premise Paulogia disputed through oral development and literary dependence. Live burden: McLatchie therefore needed independent support for source proximity and transmission before encounter detail or persecution could exclude alternatives, while allowing that mixed or gradually developing explanations might cross categories. Locked score: 79/100 — The framework was coherent and responsive to the motion, but its most controversial historical premise remained insufficiently established, warranting strong credit without an established conclusion.
moves.words: In his final synthesis, McLatchie organizes the case around resurrection, honest mistake, and deceit, with source reliability governing both exclusions in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia’s opening mapped an accuracy-and-sincerity spectrum and emphasized that Christianity could begin through sincere mistake, embellishment, or fabrication without a physical resurrection, exposing the weakness of any necessity claim. Principal limitation: Yet the motion asked which explanation is best, and his early demand that every nonresurrection point be impossible substituted possibility for comparative probability until his closing statement finally endorsed naturalistic preference. Live burden: He consequently retained the burden to identify a concrete natural pathway, connect it to the surviving evidence, and compare its explanatory costs against McLatchie’s cumulative case rather than keeping alternatives open. Locked score: 70/100 — The opening deserves 70 because it created underdetermination and framed rival classes, but its burden standard was misaligned with the proposition and delayed the positive comparison Paulogia ultimately needed.
moves.words: Paulogia’s opening summary maps natural origins across sincerity and accuracy, but initially emphasizes their possibility rather than a developed probability comparison in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia directly asked whether McLatchie accepted that natural explanations fit the evidence and, if not, what completely dismissed a single sincerely mistaken originator, forcing clarity about the resurrection claim’s intended strength. Principal limitation: The request still set complete dismissal as the target, although a best-explanation case need only make the rival less probable rather than impossible. Live burden: For this narrow challenge, Paulogia needed only expose that McLatchie had not excluded sincere error; supporting his chosen naturalistic preference required additional evidence that the hypothesis fits the sources better. Locked score: 63/100 — The move effectively tested overstatement and preserved a live alternative, but its impossibility framing did little to rank the historically salient competing explanations or explain why natural fit should receive greater comparative weight.
moves.words: Paulogia directly asks McLatchie either to accept naturalistic fit or identify evidence that completely dismisses a sincerely mistaken single-origin hypothesis in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia’s closing met the wording of the motion by stating that a naturalistic explanation was the best option and tied that preference to Gospel dependence, elaboration, and failures of transfer from mundane accuracy to supernatural claims. Principal limitation: The conclusion remained broader than its support, because thousands of possible explanations do not collectively raise the probability of any account, and his favored story was sparsely specified. Live burden: He needed to show how the initiating error survived transmission into multiple bodily encounter narratives and why that developmental pathway was more probable than McLatchie’s account after granting interconnections. Locked score: 78/100 — The score of 78 recognizes a position and a warning about cross-domain transfer, while reflecting that the comparative naturalistic model arrived late and never received comparable development.
moves.words: Paulogia’s closing endorses naturalistic explanation, retains the single-mistake hypothesis, and rejects automatic transfer from mundane textual accuracy to resurrection testimony in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie’s foot-washing example produced an interlocking detail: Luke supplies the dispute over greatness that explains Jesus washing the disciples’ feet in John, although neither writer overtly constructs the connection. Principal limitation: This is evidence of remembered circumstances or shared historical material, but the fit can arise through tradition, source knowledge, or narrative development and does not by itself identify eyewitness authorship. Live burden: He had to establish independence and casualness across examples, then explain why reliability in ministry episodes should increase confidence in resurrection appearances rather than only in a historical kernel. Locked score: 79/100 — The move earns 79 because its textual observation is specific and probative against pure invention, while alternative transmission routes and the later supernatural inference limit how much evidential weight it can carry.
moves.words: McLatchie links John’s foot-washing episode with Luke’s dispute over greatness, presenting their incidental fit as evidence of connected historical circumstances in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia offered a transmission mechanism in which persuasive details survive, objections invite elaboration, Mark records traditions, and Matthew, Luke, and John reshape earlier material, challenging an eyewitness interpretation of interconnections. Principal limitation: The model fits literary dependence generally, yet in this debate it was mostly asserted and illustrated through analogy rather than shown to generate McLatchie’s examples without deliberate coordination. Live burden: His remaining burden was to distinguish oral selection from post hoc accommodation, date the additions, and show how development explains both casual cross-account fits and the resurrection narratives without assuming every useful detail was selected. Locked score: 75/100 — At 75, the move supplies a competing process and exposes underdetermination, but its causal particulars remain less demonstrated than the confidence of Paulogia’s evolutionary description suggests.
moves.words: Paulogia proposes oral selection, embellishment, and literary dependence as mechanisms explaining persuasive detail without granting eyewitness authorship or independent resurrection testimony in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie improved the undesigned-coincidence argument by focusing on casual, artless details such as the Passover chronology across Mark and John, arguing that readers commonly miss the fit and that neither account appears written to explain the other. Principal limitation: This criterion gives a reason to distinguish historical interlock from obvious harmonization, although subtlety alone cannot exclude common tradition, indirect dependence, editorial compression, or coincidences discovered through selective comparison. Live burden: He needed a controlled set showing that such fits occur more specifically under independent access than under literary development, and he had to connect chronology to resurrection testimony. Locked score: 83/100 — The locked 83 reflects a discriminator with real evidential value, tempered by unresolved base-rate and selection concerns and by the limited transfer from mundane narrative detail.
moves.words: McLatchie argues that subtle Passover chronology, which neither Mark nor John overtly explains, distinguishes remembered interlock from designed literary harmonization in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia located the decisive hinge in McLatchie’s maximal-data reply: multisensory encounters resist mistake only if the Gospel authors or their sources reliably preserve what purported eyewitnesses reported. Principal limitation: Withholding assent from that premise weakened McLatchie’s inference, but Paulogia did not fully engage the positive authorship, interconnection, Pauline, and Acts considerations offered to support source proximity. Live burden: His narrow rebuttal needed only show that eyewitness transmission remained underdetermined; his broader natural preference required some affirmative reason to favor development rather than treating uncertainty itself as evidence. Locked score: 87/100 — This precise challenge substantially constrained the trilemma, while its limited engagement with McLatchie’s cumulative source case prevented an even higher score.
moves.words: Paulogia challenges whether Gospel writers or their sources were connected to eyewitnesses, making vivid encounter detail conditional on a disputed historical premise.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie candidly granted a candidate discrepancy between Mark and John and analyzed its two epistemic directions: contradiction reduces reliability, while divergent presentation can support independence and thereby strengthen some interconnections. Principal limitation: This avoided simplistic harmonization and showed that features may cut differently, but independence inferred from disagreement does not guarantee truth, nor does every discrepancy license credit for independent attestation. Live burden: He had to estimate whether the positive independence signal outweighed the negative accuracy cost in the relevant passages and demonstrate that the sources were independent where resurrection evidence mattered. Locked score: 88/100 — The move merits 88 because it was balanced, responsive, and methodologically mature, with the remaining deduction reflecting the absence of a calibrated net assessment rather than any failure to acknowledge contrary evidence.
moves.words: McLatchie grants that discrepancy reduces reliability while arguing that divergent presentation can independently support source independence, giving the same feature opposing evidential effects.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia’s Star Wars comparison demonstrated the logical point that independently presented details can interlock within an invented or developed narrative world, so an undesigned coincidence does not entail historical truth. Principal limitation: The analogy captured how audience questions and successive retellings might supply explanatory details, but a deliberately coordinated multimedia franchise differs from ancient oral transmission and cannot establish equal probabilities. Live burden: He needed historical evidence that the Gospel tradition underwent the objection-driven elaboration and a criterion explaining when casualness ceases to favor independent memory over adaptive storytelling. Locked score: 83/100 — The score of 83 reflects a memorable and relevant defeater to overclaiming, balanced against the analogy’s limited historical fit and its inability by itself to explain the particular distribution of Gospel agreements and differences.
moves.words: Paulogia’s Star Wars analogy shows that separately presented fictional details can interlock, so explanatory coherence alone does not establish historical truth in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie explained the inferential bridge: ordinary confirmations would support the Gospel writers as informed and truthful, which would then justify using their resurrection encounters to evaluate honest mistake and using persecution to evaluate deceit. Principal limitation: This is more careful than claiming that one accurate detail proves every supernatural report, yet the bridge remains probabilistic and vulnerable to compartmental accuracy, theological elaboration, and unequal source quality across episodes. Live burden: He needed to quantify or compare how mundane confirmations raise confidence in the appearance material, while securing the persecution premise and defending the conditional use of Acts. Locked score: 84/100 — The locked 84 rewards a coherent architecture that answers the relevance question, but preserves a deduction because the contested transfer is the very step Paulogia never granted.
moves.words: McLatchie argues that ordinary textual confirmations support authorial reliability, allowing encounter detail and costly proclamation to bear respectively on mistake and deceit.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia distinguished granting accurate ministry material from accepting resurrection narratives, correctly insisting that reliability in one part of a document does not automatically validate another part’s supernatural report. Principal limitation: Blocking automatic transfer did not show that confirmed mundane detail supplies no probabilistic support for an author’s access, care, or truthfulness elsewhere. Live burden: For the immediate objection, Paulogia needed only prevent McLatchie’s cross-domain inference from becoming decisive; to support naturalistic preference, he also needed grounds for treating the appearance material as later elaboration rather than partly independent testimony. Locked score: 89/100 — The distinction exposed a central inferential gap with exceptional clarity, although it left room for a calibrated, source-specific reliability update.
moves.words: Paulogia distinguishes accurate ministry kernels from resurrection reports, denying that mundane historical success automatically authenticates a document’s supernatural claims in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie argued that public group appearances, conversations, touch, eating, and repeated events across forty days would be difficult for the witnesses to misperceive, giving the honest-mistake horn concrete evidential pressure. Principal limitation: The force of this argument is conditional on the later Gospel descriptions preserving early testimony; without that premise, narrative detail measures the final texts rather than the originating experience that Paulogia hypothesized. Live burden: He therefore still had to establish source proximity and independence strongly enough to block hallucination, misidentification, visionary interpretation, and gradual embellishment at the historical stage. Locked score: 80/100 — The score of 80 reflects substantial explanatory power once the reports are admitted and a clear answer to vague mistake proposals, discounted because the crucial authenticity condition remained disputed throughout the debate.
moves.words: McLatchie argues that repeated multisensory group encounters resist honest mistake, provided the Gospel descriptions substantially preserve what earliest witnesses reported in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia identified a candidate in which one sincere but mistaken individual, Peter, initiates resurrection belief, thereby showing why later willingness to suffer need not imply that the original interpretation was accurate. Principal limitation: The proposal remained a sketch: it did not specify the initial experience, the transition to a bodily claim, the role of Paul and other named witnesses, or the growth of detailed encounter traditions. Live burden: To become a comparative explanation, it needed support and a transmission account demonstrating that one error predicts the available texts better than resurrection or several independent experiences. Locked score: 69/100 — The score of 69 credits its focused challenge to an inference from sincerity to truth, while marking the gap between a logically possible origin and a developed, evidence-sensitive rival.
moves.words: Paulogia proposes one sincerely mistaken originator, possibly Peter, as a natural starting point, while leaving later bodily elaboration largely unspecified in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie answered the sincere-origin challenge by conceding that minimal facts leave open experience types and then arguing that maximal Gospel data provide the multisensory, conversational, repeated encounters needed to resist honest mistake. Principal limitation: This was a qualification rather than an evasion, and it exposed why First Corinthians alone cannot carry his conclusion, but it increased dependence on contested Gospel authorship and transmission reliability. Live burden: His remaining burden was to prove that these detailed reports are early, independent, and unembellished enough to describe the witnesses rather than reflect narrative development. Locked score: 86/100 — The move earns 86 for diagnosing the minimal-facts weakness and offering a conditional response, with the deduction reflecting that its discriminatory power arrives only after acceptance of the debate’s most disputed source premise.
moves.words: McLatchie rejects minimal-facts underdetermination and relies on richer Gospel encounters because First Corinthians permits many different originating experience types in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie used voluntary hardships, imprisonments, dangers, and conduct to argue that early proclaimers sincerely believed their resurrection testimony, appropriately directing the evidence against deliberate deception rather than treating suffering as proof of truth. Principal limitation: The initial formulation spoke broadly of apostles and leaned on Paley, leaving uncertain which witnesses made which claims, what costs they knowingly accepted, and how those links are documented. Live burden: He still needed named, source-specific chains connecting an alleged eyewitness to a resurrection assertion and voluntary persistence under avoidable pressure, while separating later Christian persecution from first-generation evidence. Locked score: 76/100 — The score of 76 recognizes the valid sincerity principle and cumulative relevance, but reflects that broad categories of costly proclamation did not yet meet Paulogia’s demand for discriminating particulars.
moves.words: McLatchie argues that voluntary hardship supports early proclaimers’ sincerity, although his initial formulation lacks secure witness-by-witness links among experience, testimony, and risk.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: After McLatchie had already narrowed martyrdom, Paulogia’s Acts-aside hypothetical demanded names, precise resurrection claims, reliable preaching evidence, and documented risk, exposing gaps that broad references to apostles can conceal. Principal limitation: Temporarily setting Acts aside clarified source dependence but could not establish that its evidence was worthless, and a sincerity case can draw on nonfatal hardship without requiring an execution choice. Live burden: Paulogia needed only show that generic persecution claims lacked secure witness-specific links; favoring his natural account further required explaining how the remaining named evidence fits sincere mistake. Locked score: 90/100 — The questioning exercised excellent source control and burden discipline, with a small deduction for pressing the hypothetical beyond what it alone could establish.
moves.words: After McLatchie narrows martyrdom, Paulogia asks hypothetically without Acts which named eyewitnesses demonstrably preached resurrection claims and placed themselves at risk in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie declined a sweeping martyrdom argument, limited the named deaths, acknowledged Nero’s political motives and uncertain recantation opportunities, and appealed instead to voluntarily endured danger and imprisonment. Principal limitation: The modest case still depended substantially on Acts and on connecting particular sufferers to resurrection testimony, but conditional use of a contested source was not automatically circular. Live burden: He needed to defend Acts’ reliability for these episodes and distinguish voluntary exposure for testimony from generalized hostility, while keeping the conclusion confined to sincerity rather than resurrection truth. Locked score: 85/100 — The careful concessions produced a defensible argument, although source dependence and incomplete person-by-person linkage limited its overall comparative force in this debate.
moves.words: McLatchie limits persecution evidence to general hardship supporting sincerity, conceding sparse martyrdom evidence, political motives, and uncertain opportunities to recant in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia emphasized that persecution can support sincerity while leaving honest mistake untouched, and his question whether even five people could be mistaken prevented commitment from being treated as factual accuracy. Principal limitation: Establishing that collective mistake remains possible did not assess how probable it would be if several detailed, repeated, partly independent encounters were granted. Live burden: His narrow reply succeeded by preserving the mistake horn; support for naturalistic preference required showing why the contested witness and encounter evidence fails to reduce mistake enough, without having to prove one complete causal history. Locked score: 91/100 — The logical limitation on persecution evidence was decisive, with the remaining deduction reflecting incomplete engagement with McLatchie’s conditional maximal-data case.
moves.words: Paulogia stresses that sincere suffering cannot distinguish accurate belief from honest error, even if several named proclaimers voluntarily accepted danger in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie argued that miracles must deviate from nature to function as divine signs and that Christian evidence—Paul’s conversion, prophecy, Jesus’ identity claims, contemporary miracles, and Israel—could raise the prior probability of resurrection. Principal limitation: This supplied a coherent Bayesian response to automatic dismissal, but most supporting categories were mentioned rather than defended within the debate and risked expanding the case far beyond the shared evidential record. Live burden: He still had to show that these considerations genuinely favor Christian divine action without presupposing disputed theology, and then combine that prior with the reliability of the resurrection testimony. Locked score: 75/100 — The score of 75 recognizes a relevant framework and religious-context explanation, while heavily discounting unsupported auxiliary claims that could not bear their assigned prior-shifting role here.
moves.words: McLatchie argues that divine signs must deviate from nature and invokes wider Christian evidence to raise resurrection’s prior probability above automatic exclusion.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia highlighted the frequency of error and deception against the rarity of miracles, explaining why testimonial failure initially appears more probable than resurrection and why Gospel testimony faces a demanding threshold. Principal limitation: This is a legitimate prior-probability concern, but his initial formulation approached an absolute ceiling and compared raw daily frequencies without accounting for evidence quality, independence, specificity, or divine-context hypotheses; his later uncertainty qualified that stance. Live burden: He needed a calibrated account of how the prior should update under different conditions and an assessment of the sources without converting methodological naturalism into an absolute prohibition. Locked score: 76/100 — The score of 76 credits the probabilistic challenge and its relevance to best explanation, while reflecting an overstatement that McLatchie could correctly identify as mathematically untenable.
moves.words: Paulogia contrasts common error and deception with rare miracles, setting a demanding testimonial threshold that his later answer explicitly leaves uncertain in this exchange.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie replied that if testimony provides any likelihood advantage for a proposition, sufficiently strong testimony can in principle overcome a low prior, exposing the mathematical problem with an absolute testimonial barrier. Principal limitation: The response established an updating rule but did not show that these Gospel reports possess the needed independence, reliability, and likelihood ratio, which remained the historical dispute. Live burden: He had to translate his arguments into a comparative case strong enough to cross Paulogia’s stated high threshold and account for the disputed dependence among accounts. Locked score: 91/100 — The score of 91 rewards a concise, rigorous correction with philosophical force, while stopping short of full credit because proving that testimony can overcome a prior is not demonstrating that the testimony offered here actually does.
moves.words: McLatchie explains that sufficiently strong testimony can mathematically overcome a low prior without yet showing that these contested Gospel accounts reach that threshold.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia stated genuine uncertainty about whether testimony could ever suffice, allowed that one hundred independent cases might show something happened, and returned attention to disputed dependence among the Gospels. Principal limitation: This uncertainty avoided a categorical impossibility claim but left his updating standard unclear, including how independence, quality, and causal attribution would change his confidence. Live burden: He did not need a complete natural causal reconstruction merely to withhold assent; to justify his stated naturalistic preference, he needed a more explicit comparison showing why the present, allegedly dependent reports remain below a reasonable threshold. Locked score: 86/100 — The qualification was candid and source-sensitive, though the absence of a stable updating rule limited its affirmative force as support for naturalistic preference.
moves.words: Paulogia remains uncertain about testimonial sufficiency, allows hypothetical independent cases to matter, and argues that disputed Gospel dependence prevents comparable cumulative force here.

strengths: McLatchie corrected the central burden from deductive necessity to comparative probability and kept his later case focused on the best-explanation question.
He integrated source interconnections, detailed encounters, and costly proclamation into a cumulative trilemma rather than treating any single consideration as decisive.
He made unusually careful concessions about discrepancies, minimal-facts underdetermination, martyrdom evidence, Nero’s motives, and the limited role of persecution.

blunders.text: His case depended heavily on the contested transfer from mundane textual reliability to the authenticity of detailed resurrection narratives without sufficiently calibrating that transfer.
Several claims offered to raise the miracle prior—prophecy, contemporary miracles, Israel, and Jesus’ identity claims—were introduced without enough debate-specific defense.

strengths: Paulogia repeatedly separated sincerity from truth and showed why persecution cannot resolve the live possibility of honest mistake.
He exposed the dependence of the maximal-data case on eyewitness proximity and rejected any automatic move from accurate historical kernels to supernatural accuracy.
His Acts-aside request for named witnesses, precise claims, and documented risks tested the narrowed persecution case without confusing nonfatal hardship with martyrdom.

blunders.text: His opening often treated the survival of any natural possibility as sufficient, even though the motion required a comparative case for the best explanation.

His favored single-sincere-origin hypothesis remained underdescribed, weakening its support for naturalistic preference even though withholding assent did not require a complete causal reconstruction.

finalArgument.thesis: McLatchie can strengthen his cumulative case by separating three updates that the debate sometimes compressed: textual access, resistance to mistake, and evidence of sincerity.
premises: Casual interconnections and resistant discrepancies support partial independence when their distribution is less expected under direct copying or deliberate harmonization.
That independence matters most when it appears inside the resurrection material, because accuracy in ministry narratives transfers only probabilistically across subject matter.
Reports of repeated group conversation, touch, and eating lower the plausibility of simple misidentification in proportion to their proximity to witness testimony.
Voluntarily endured danger updates sincerity rather than truth, so it narrows fabrication without being counted again as evidence against honest error.
Religious context can modify the resurrection prior, but only through considerations defended independently of the resurrection evidence under evaluation.
finalArgument.conclusion: Keeping those updates separate reveals the exact cumulative claim: source proximity licenses encounter content, encounter content pressures mistake, and costly proclamation pressures deceit, leaving resurrection comparatively stronger without claiming necessity.

newArguments.title: Distributional Independence Test
newArguments.text: Instead of treating every interconnection as equal, compare where subtle fits and genuine discrepancies occur across the documents. Independent memory predicts uneven agreement, incidental chronology, and unforced explanatory links alongside mistakes; direct copying predicts closer verbal or structural dependence; later harmonization predicts conspicuous repairs. Applying those rival predictions specifically to resurrection passages would determine whether mundane interconnections legitimately raise confidence in encounter content.

newArguments.title: Sequential Horn Updating
newArguments.text: The trilemma should be evaluated as a sequence of conditional updates rather than three labels. First estimate whether the reports preserve early witness claims; then ask what those reported experiences imply about mistake; only afterward use voluntary hardship to update deception. This prevents source confidence, encounter detail, and sincerity from being counted repeatedly while showing exactly which evidential link must carry each part of the resurrection inference.

finalArgument.thesis: Paulogia’s strongest extension is an underdetermination argument: McLatchie’s evidence loses discriminatory force whenever the same observation is reasonably expected under ordinary transmission.
premises: Mundane accuracy can survive oral transmission and literary reuse even when supernatural scenes acquire additional detail, so cross-domain transfer requires separate justification.
Sincere belief explains willingness to preach and suffer under both truth and mistake, making persecution largely neutral between those two hypotheses.
Disputed dependence reduces the multiplication of testimonial force because several texts may preserve variations of a shared tradition rather than separate witness access.
A detailed single-origin history would strengthen naturalistic preference, but criticism of McLatchie requires only showing that his evidence does not discriminate as strongly as claimed.
Testimony can overcome a low prior in principle, while the present disagreement concerns whether these particular sources supply enough independence, proximity, and specificity.
finalArgument.conclusion: This approach supports a naturalistic preference through comparative modesty: ordinary transmission uses familiar processes and remains compatible with the evidence, while McLatchie’s added source-authentication steps retain substantial unresolved uncertainty.

newArguments.title: Transmission Gradient Prediction
newArguments.text: A developed sincere-error model predicts a traceable gradient from earlier sparse formulations to later concrete scenes, with additions clustering around apologetic pressures such as mistaken identity, physicality, and group verification. Testing that pattern across First Corinthians and the Gospel strata would give Paulogia a positive explanatory measure. A stable early distribution of the same difficult details across independent sources would count strongly against the model.

newArguments.title: Witness Link Matrix
newArguments.text: Construct a separate chain for every proposed witness: claimed experience, earliest attestation, access of the reporting source, public proclamation, documented hardship, and opportunity to avoid that hardship. Empty links would prevent generic references to apostles from accumulating unwarranted force, while completed links would constrain the single-origin theory. This method converts the persecution disagreement into auditable evidence and preserves the crucial distinction between sincerity and accuracy.

editorialReview.sourceFidelity: I checked every summary, description, critique, and extension against the direct debate material while excluding audience questions, logistics, promotions, and corrupted transcript clauses.
editorialReview.completeQuotes: I verified that both featured quotations reproduce complete eligible thoughts exactly: McLatchie’s comparative resurrection conclusion and Paulogia’s naturalistic preference.
editorialReview.scoreConsistency: I confirmed the 83–80 overall result and preserved every one of the twenty-five locked move scores without recalculation, substitution, or drift.
editorialReview.nonformulaicCritiques: I reviewed paired critiques together and ensured each explains a move-specific strength, limitation, unresolved burden, and score rationale from its actual exchange.
editorialReview.aiContributionNonformulaic: I checked that the four AI extensions add distinct testable reasoning through distribution, sequential updating, transmission gradients, and witness-link analysis.
editorialReview.aiPunctuation: I reviewed the AI prose for natural sentence structure and punctuation, avoiding mirrored scaffolds, fragments, canned transitions, and mechanical sentence-bank construction.
editorialReview.referenceComparison: I compared the final evaluation with the supplied reference metrics only for calibration and did not import claims, scores, or language from another debate.
